**Code evidence:**

- MEASURED, chat_runner.py:1503-1535: the staged envelope is prepended as a labelled preamble plus fence_untrusted(snapshot, source='investigate:<kind>'), and the docstring states the reason rather than the rule — 'Entity snapshots contain external/LLM-authored text (an email body, a loop finding), so the fence is NON-NEGOTIABLE: the model reads the envelope as quoted DATA, never instructions'
- 🔑 THE ONCE-ONLY GUARD IS THE DATA, NOT A FLAG: after the first turn the code REWRITES the staged context keeping only kind/title/back_link and DROPPING the snapshot — 'the injection guard, so later turns inject nothing'. A boolean could be missed on a new code path; an absent snapshot cannot be injected
- the display fields deliberately survive because 'the header ContextChip reads kind/title/back_link for the session's whole life' — so the guard is scoped to the payload rather than to the whole envelope
- ':1514 This is the ONE injection point — no resolver output may reach a prompt any other way'
- tests/test_investigate.py 36/36

**Notes:** 🔑 ARCC'S ONE TRANSFERABLE LINE LANDS EXACTLY HERE. Its Bedrock guardrail guidance says a prompt-attack filter only works if 'builder teams must apply INPUT TAGS to user prompt portion' — i.e. the untrusted span must be delimited for any control to govern it. This codebase agrees on the mechanism (delimit the span) and differs on what acts on it: a managed classifier there, structural containment here. For a self-hosted instance the fence is the better half of that trade, because its correctness is assertable rather than probabilistic.
